title: Selected Stabilizer Subspaces for Compact Many-Body Wave Functions
abstract: Selected configuration interaction (SCI) obtains accurate many-body solutions by variationally diagonalising the Hamiltonian in a sparse, iteratively selected set of configurations, but can lose compactness when the target state has broad configurational support. We introduce selected stabilizer interaction (SSI), a fully classical, SCI-inspired method that instead iteratively constructs a nonorthogonal subspace spanned by a systematically enlargeable set of selected stabilizer states. A single stabilizer, generated by Clifford operations, can encode a structured superposition of (possibly exponentially) many configurations, shifting the relevant compression from configurational to stabilizer sparsity. We benchmark ground-state energies, fidelities, superposition degrees and required expansion lengths against exact diagonalization and equivalent SCI schemes for the transverse-field Ising, XXZ Heisenberg, and Hubbard models, finding particularly strong compression from the stabilizer representation in the spin models, and increasing advantage with system size for these systems. The results establish a proof of principle for heuristic selected stabilizer diagonalization, while also identifying particular challenges in symmetry handling and effective exploration of the stabilizer space.
summary: This paper introduces Selected Stabilizer Interaction (SSI), a novel, classical method to approximate quantum many-body wavefunctions by expanding them in a basis of stabilizer states. It successfully shifts the computational bottleneck from managing exponentially large configuration spaces to managing the sparsity of the stabilizer representation. The results prove the concept using spin models, suggesting a viable path for simulating complex quantum systems beyond the reach of standard configuration interaction methods.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in quantum many-body simulations, which limits high-accuracy calculations.
main_result: The proposed Selected Stabilizer Interaction (SSI) method successfully shifts the required computational compression from the configurational basis to the stabilizer sparsity, showing strong compression advantages, especially in spin models.
method: SSI is a classical, SCI-inspired technique that iteratively constructs a nonorthogonal subspace spanned by selected stabilizer states, allowing for efficient representation of complex wavefunctions.
model_or_system: The method is benchmarked on several quantum many-body models, including the transverse-field Ising, XXZ Heisenberg, and Hubbard models, applicable to general n-qubit quantum states.
key_observables: Ground-state energies, fidelities, superposition degrees, and the required expansion length (comparing SSI vs. SCI vs. exact diagonalization).
important_parameters: System size (n), interaction strengths (e.g., U/t for Hubbard model), and the structure of the Pauli operators used for stabilization.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the wavefunction can be accurately represented by a compact, systematically generated set of stabilizer states, though challenges remain in symmetry handling and fermionic systems.
figures_summary: Figure B1 compares the required expansion length for SSI versus SCI for the 1D Hubbard chain, demonstrating the potential advantage of the stabilizer representation over the configurational one.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the SSI concept, details the mathematical framework using stabilizer states and Clifford operations, presents algorithms for overlap calculation (STABCIRC, CONJCIRC), and benchmarks the method against established models.
why_interesting: For theoretical physicists working on many-body dynamics, this offers a powerful, classically tractable alternative to standard exponential basis set expansions, providing a new route for simulating strongly correlated systems.

Candidates are then generated as described in Section III B 1 and ranked according to a residual as described in Section III B 2. The top candidate is added to the stabilizer basis and a new trial wavefunction is obtained by diagonalization (see Section III B 3). The process is repeated until the energy change is below some convergence threshold.
